comment: Falsifiability registry: every step in VALIDATE_STEPS ∪ STOP_HOOK_STEPS must carry at least one mechanical proof that it CAN go red. Proof kinds: 'fixture' (a repo test file that spawns the real gate and asserts exit 1 — ref must exist), 'selftest' (a literal step/leg title that must appear in .github/workflows/selftest.yml or in a scripts/ci/* helper that workflow invokes — the W6 emulator legs live in bash files because the emulator-runner action execs its script under dash), 'runner' (the step wraps a vendor tool whose non-zero exit is the red; OUR wiring's failure propagation is proven by the validate-runner tests — ref must exist). scripts/check-canary-coverage.mjs enforces bidirectional closure: an unregistered step OR a stale registry entry reds the PR that caused it. Guard-rule falsifiability is a PER-RULE closure, not a count: check-canary-coverage.mjs imports the pure-data rule tables from .claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs (BASH_RULES, WRITE_PROTECTED, WRITE_GLOBAL_CHECKS) and asserts every rule id has a behavioral deny/allow case (a RULE_CANARIES entry) in tests/hooks/hook-contract.test.mjs — a rule added without a canary reds the PR. hookRules below keeps only a human-readable grep-able deny example per surface. W6 ARMED the deferred device/runtime canaries in real selftest jobs: the broken-testID sweep red + agent-chain green (maestro-smoke Canary 19), the 300ms busy-loop perf-marker red (maestro-smoke Canary 20), the keyset-index-drop STRUCTURAL red (bootstrap-linux Canary 17 — pgTAP's owner-leading-column assertion, NOT a plan probe: this header called it one for two releases, and the distinction is the whole reason Canary 24 exists. Canary 17 must drop the keyset index AND the primary key, because pgTAP is satisfied by either carrying the leading column; Canary 24 drops only the secondary index and reds db-perf on plan SHAPE while Canary 17's assertion stays green), the strip-Authorization live-suite red (integration Canary C01), and the nondeterministic-plugin prebuild-compare red (bootstrap-linux Canary 18). What remains CI-cadence-honest rather than per-PR: the emulator canaries live in a schedule/dispatch-only job (cost), stated in the lane notes below.

schema-rls.ref: Canary 5: remove FORCE RLS from the migration → schema-rls must FAIL

schema-rls.note: 0.6.0 adds the POLICY -> GRANT closure, registered here rather than as a new step because it is the same gate consuming a parse it already ran. Table privileges are checked BEFORE row security, so a policy naming a role that holds no privilege on the table is UNREACHABLE CODE that reads in review as a granted one: the statement raises 42501 (PostgREST: HTTP 403) before any policy is consulted. This gate has called parseGrants since 0.2.0 and used only the FUNCTION half of it, for the SECURITY DEFINER EXECUTE surface; the TABLE half was dead output, so a table shipping ENABLE + FORCE + four per-operation policies + both isolation registries + an owner-column index and NO GRANT STATEMENT ANYWHERE was fully green -- and every fixture in this gate's own test file was exactly that shape. WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE, AND WHY IT IS DATED: Supabase's default privileges grant anon/authenticated/service_role on every newly created table in `public`, so the omission WORKS -- the default already handed the role its privileges -- and it stops working for projects created on or after 2026-10-30, when those defaults stop being applied and the auto_expose_new_tables switch that would have restored them is itself removed on the same date. The same migration file therefore passes review, passes this gate, works in the project it was written against, and 403s in the next project it is replayed into, byte-identical in both. THE INJECTIONS: deleting the GRANT from the fixture reds FOUR times, once per operation, each naming the date, the SQLSTATE and the exact GRANT statement that discharges it; deleting one grant line from the SHIPPED notes migration reds the real scaffold, which is what makes the shipped-tree green non-vacuous; a later REVOKE undoing an earlier GRANT reds for that operation ONLY, because the history is folded in STATEMENT ORDER and the shipped idiom is REVOKE-then-narrow-GRANT; and a SCHEMA grant is refused as a TABLE grant, which is the name collision the audit migration's `REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA audit FROM anon, authenticated, service_role` would otherwise have caused. THREE CARVE-OUTS, each load-bearing and each with its own GREEN proof, because a gate that reds correct SQL gets deleted: a policy whose predicate is literally `false` needs no grant (the shipped tenancy spine's deny-all writes), a RESTRICTIVE policy carries no reachability claim since it only ever subtracts rows, and a policy with no TO clause names no role to close over. THE REVERSE DIRECTION IS DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED: `GRANT SELECT, DELETE ON TABLE public.orgs TO service_role` is a legitimate ADR-governed grant with no policy behind it, because service_role BYPASSES row security -- a grant=>policy rule would red the shipped tree for being correct. Ramped from baseVersion 0.6.0 until 0.7.0, unlike the two unramped negation checks above it: this one has a real legacy population (a pre-flip project where the missing grant genuinely works), and rampNote prints every finding as a NOTE for as long as it is armed. 0.9.9 adds THE MFA RAIL to the same fixture file, registered here rather than as a new step because it is the same gate consuming a parse it already ran. The closure is over the rail SHAPE, never its coverage — which tables warrant a second factor is a product decision — and it exists because the vendor-documented aal2 policy is broken in two directions with the second one silent: read as the invoker it raises 42501 for everyone; "fixed" with a GRANT on auth.mfa_factors the table is still RLS-enabled with no policy, so the count is 0 for ENROLLED users too, the CASE falls through to array[aal1,aal2] and the policy admits aal1. Reds proven: the grant itself (named as the fail-open it is), a PERMISSIVE MFA policy, a per-operation one (Supabase’s own second docs page writes this policy `for update`, gating writes and leaving SELECT open), USING without WITH CHECK, a deleted runtime proof, and helpers defined with NO policy using them. Plus the hole the rail would have opened: a RESTRICTIVE policy no longer satisfies the per-operation requirement, because a policy that can only SUBTRACT grants nothing — unreachable until this release seeded the tree’s first restrictive policy. The EXECUTED twin is supabase/tests/mfa_aal2.test.sql, which was run against a live stack both ways: green on the shipped rail, and red on the vendor policy with the two rows an enrolled aal1 session should not have seen.

schema-rls.ref: Canary 22: RLS turned OFF by a later migration → schema-rls must FAIL

tenancy.note: The predicate schema-rls provably cannot judge: `org_id = (SELECT auth.uid())` — a tenant column compared to a user id — is REAL by every schema-rls rule and isolates nothing; here it reds against the closed predicateForms set printing the exact normalized predicate. Also proven red: a top-level OR arm without a scope term (the `... OR owner_id = (SELECT auth.uid())` re-opening), the correlated-argument ban (`private.member_rank(org_id)` — a per-row SubPlan wrapped in `(SELECT` that passes every wrapper check), an off-scale rank floor, a relation sub-select, a nullable/FK-less tenant key, a UNIQUE omitting the tenant column, a missing/disarmable freeze trigger, a seat-table SELECT policy that calls the helpers (recursion smell — the 42P17 probe is the proof), a self-keyed membership INSERT to authenticated (self-granted seats), definer/parameterized/non-STABLE helpers, and a nonPublicSchemas schema published in [api].schemas. THE SILENT-NO-OP PROOF (the one no other layer can reach): a rank-scoped write policy TO the rpc writer role with no PAIRED self-only SELECT policy on the seat table reds — because the rank helper is SECURITY INVOKER, reads the seat table as that role, hits RLS default-deny, returns an empty map, and every seat change then matches ZERO ROWS AND SUCCEEDS. Valid SQL, present policy, reviewed predicate shape, and promotions in production that silently do nothing. THE ORG-TABLE PROOF: public.orgs carries no tenant column, so column-driven discovery never reaches it — `USING (created_by = (SELECT auth.uid()) OR name IS NOT NULL)` passes every other static gate in the repo while publishing every org row to every user; the explicit org-table pass (scope column substituted to its own primary key) reds it. Anti-vacuity: empty predicateForms, malformed JSON, missing sections, reasonless table-narrowed forms and reasonless/stale escapes all FAIL CLOSED; a table-narrowed form does not license the same predicate on another table; the adoption ramp covers only the no-tenant-column upgrade path, and a REGRESSION case pins that an ancient baseVersion cannot disarm findings once the surface exists. 0.9.9 strengthens the RUNTIME twin (supabase/tests/audit_immutability.test.sql, now 32 assertions) rather than the static gate: service_role — the role that bypasses RLS and the one an Edge Function actually holds — ATTEMPTS read, forge, modify, delete and truncate instead of having its refusal inferred from has_table_privilege, which is a statement about pg_class rather than about the system, and the difference is ASD's POOR-vs-EXCELLENT evidence tier. The forged INSERT carries a real org_id (built before the role switch, stashed in a transaction-local GUC) because an INSERT a NOT NULL constraint would refuse whoever ran it proves nothing about privilege. RED PROVEN AGAINST A LIVE STACK, and it corrected the design assumption: granting service_role USAGE plus full DML reds EXACTLY the read and the forged insert and leaves UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE passing, because the layer-3 and layer-4 triggers refuse those with every grant in place — so reading and forging are held by the grant ALONE, and 'just grant the Edge Function read access to the audit table' is the single likeliest edit these two assertions exist to catch.

migrations.ref: Canary 3: edit a committed migration → migrations must FAIL

db-limits.note: The blast-radius controls, proven falsifiable in the two directions a catalog assertion cannot reach. STATEMENT ORDER: a later `ALTER ROLE ... RESET` (or a re-SET to a wider value) vacates an earlier ceiling, so the matrix is folded in migration order rather than searched for a matching line — a gate that only greps for the SET stays green on a role whose ceiling was removed three migrations later. INERT KNOBS RED RATHER THAN PASS: `temp_file_limit` is superuser-only and `postgres` cannot set it, and `CONNECTION LIMIT` is refused on the reserved `authenticator` and inert on anon/authenticated/service_role because they are not login roles — both were verified against a live PG17, and both are exactly the shape that reads as a control in review while doing nothing (`CONNECTION LIMIT -1`, the explicit no-limit spelling, stays green because it claims nothing). QUOTA SHAPE: a FOR EACH ROW trigger reds (it serializes every insert behind one hot tuple and turns a 1000-row load into 1000 dead tuples); a statement trigger with no `REFERENCING NEW TABLE` reds (it can only ever count zero); a RESTRICTIVE counting policy calling a STABLE function reds because it fails OPEN — the hoisted call evaluates once per statement against the PRE-statement count, so one multi-row INSERT of any size passes wholesale and the optimization defeats the control; a metered table with no trigger, and a debit with no release twin, both red. THE SILENT TOTAL FAILURE: the reconciler reassigned to the tenant-scoped writer role reds — its policies resolve through `private.member_org_ids()`, which derives from `auth.uid()`, and pg_cron runs with no JWT, so the scope array comes back EMPTY and the nightly reconcile sets every counter in the database to zero. Also red: the reconciler made client-callable, a client role granted UPDATE on the usage counter (a quota anyone can edit is not a quota), `[api].max_rows` above the reviewed cap, and a session-mode `[db.pooler]`. Anti-vacuity: malformed JSON, an EMPTY role matrix, a knob with no declared ceiling, and an `unavailable` entry without a substantive reason all FAIL CLOSED; the adoption ramp covers only the pre-0.2.0 no-settings install, and a REGRESSION case pins that an ancient baseVersion cannot disarm findings once ceilings exist.

db-limits.ref: Canary 23: a per-role ceiling reset live → the resource-limits runner must FAIL (the ceiling is not merely a row in a migration)
db-limits.note: the live direction (bootstrap-linux, a real scaffold + the Supabase local stack): tests/rls/resource-limits.test.ts. The static gate can only prove the `ALTER ROLE ... SET` is in a migration and the pgTAP twin can only prove the row landed in pg_db_role_setting — neither can prove the ceiling is IN FORCE. It is in force only because PostgREST reads pg_db_role_setting for the role it impersonates and applies those settings itself per request (`SET ROLE` alone does NOT re-apply them — verified directly). This runner calls public.effective_limits() as anon and as authenticated through PostgREST and compares what is actually in force against tools/db-limits.json, so a PostgREST upgrade that dropped the behaviour, a renamed role, or a hand-reset setting reds here while every catalog assertion stays green.

query-shapes.note: The manifest this gate judges is GENERATED BY EXECUTION — tools/gen-query-shapes.mjs drives each DAL function through a harness-owned recording Proxy and records the builder chain it produced — so the vacuity to prove against is not "the manifest is wrong" but "the manifest describes nothing": an empty manifest, an absent one, an unparseable one, and a row missing a field all FAIL CLOSED rather than judging zero shapes. The rules that matter are the ones every other check in this repo is blind to, because pgTAP's leading-column assertion, schema-rls and tenancy are all TRUE of an index that serves the filter and leaves the sort in memory: an index with the right leading column and the wrong TAIL reds; a MIXED ASC/DESC order no single scan direction can supply reds (a btree walks backwards, so the fully-reversed sort is GREEN — both directions are proven, or the rule would be a superstition); a read with no LIMIT and no aggregate reds; `.range()`/`.offset()` red BY NAME, which is why the recorder is a Proxy that captures methods no port declares rather than a fake that would crash and then be taught to ignore them; a LIMIT above [api].max_rows reds, because PostgREST truncates there silently and the has-more sentinel never arrives. THE RULE A LIVE PLAN PROBE EARNED: a keyset cursor sent as ONE top-level disjunction — the spelling every tutorial shows, the spelling this repo shipped — reds, because PostgreSQL cannot turn a top-level OR into an index range, so the cursor lands in `Filter:` and the scan still starts at the tenant's newest row. Measured on 1.1M seeded rows at page 1000, before the fix: 1115 rows removed by filter to return 21, and 1798 buffers against 8. Every structural gate was green throughout. The instrument is proven separately (value redaction, the empty-result resolution, boundKind derived rather than declared, the prefix rule, and selectSql refusing an unknown operator instead of dropping a disjunct — a dropped disjunct would EXPLAIN an easier query than the app sends).

rate-limits.note: The vacuity this gate exists for is not "the numbers are wrong" — it is a limiter that is WIRED, TESTED, AND REACHES NOTHING: a new mutation lands, nobody adds it to the policy, and the seam keeps limiting the five procedures it already knew about while the newest write path runs unbounded, with everything green. So the load-bearing proof is the CLOSURE against a GENERATED inventory (tools/generated/action-inventory.json is walked out of the composed router, never hand-written): an unmapped mutation reds, a mapping or exemption naming a procedure the router no longer exposes reds as stale, and a procedure that is BOTH mapped and exempt reds because the contract contradicts itself. THE BY-VALUE DIFF: apps/web/lib/rate-limit.ts is evaluated under node type-stripping and compared against the reviewed JSON, so a limit changed in code without a diff reds, a limit changed in the JSON that the code does not honour reds, and a documented exemption the code fails to apply reds (the worst of the three — the reason sits in the contract reading as if it were in force). An unknown name resolving to null reds, because that would make "forgot to map it" and "deliberately unlimited" the same value. THE WIRING, asserted per seam because the two share no code: dropping the `rateLimit` port from the tRPC route reds (@app/api treats a missing port as an UNLIMITED router — correct for a worker or a test, which is exactly why the absence cannot be caught from inside the router), and a Server Action with a budget it never consults reds, as does an exported *Action with no budget entry at all. Anti-vacuity: malformed JSON, an empty bucket set, a bucket or exemption with a thin reason, missing ceilings, a budget above its ceiling, a window long enough never to close, a mapping to an undeclared bucket, a declared bucket nothing spends from, and an unrecorded fail-open decision all FAIL CLOSED; the adoption ramp covers only the pre-0.2.0 tree with no budget file. THE ROUTER HALF is proven by packages/api/src/ratelimit.test.ts — a vitest suite, carried by the `unit` step rather than spawnable from here: the router half, proven against a database that THROWS if it is ever touched: a rate limit that lets the handler run and then reports the refusal has bought nothing, because the transaction, the audit row and the quota check are already paid for. Also proven: the guard rides the BASE of the ladder (notes.list, three rungs up, is refused too), the wait travels on a CLASS cause rather than a duck-typed field, a null verdict and an allowed verdict are both honoured but stay distinguishable, and the port is asked with the ACTIVE org — resolved from real seats, never from the x-org-id header a stranger could set to spend a tenant's budget. 0.10.0 ADDS THE OUTAGE-RUNG DECLARATION. The budget recorded WHETHER the limiter fails open (`decided` + `reason`) and had no way to record what limits traffic WHILE it does — so "an outage removes rate limiting entirely" and "an outage degrades to per-instance counting" were the same green, and the harness shipped the first for nine releases. `failOpen.fallback` is now required: absent reds naming why the two existing fields were not enough, a token value reds (the field wants a description, not a checkbox), a pre-0.10.0 install gets a dated NOTE until 0.11.0 because the file is a reviewed write-guarded CONSUMER artefact whose honest value depends on the deployment, and the GREEN case is the SHIPPED policy rather than a hand-mirrored fixture — so the gate reds if the template ever loses the key it demands. Found by an adversarial review, which observed that the seeded ratelimit correction had no gate to name in its seededSourceFixes entry: a seeded fix no gate reports is one a consumer never learns they owe.

backup-evidence.note: 0.9.9. THE LANE THIS ENTRY EXISTS FOR IS THE HARDEST ONE IN THE REPOSITORY TO PROVE, because it skips on every machine that has no SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN — including this harness's own CI, which has no Supabase project — so nothing in the ordinary run of things ever shows it capable of redding. The subject is not in the tree at all: backups live in the platform's control plane, which is why the live query rides a schedule and never `pnpm validate`, where a third party changing an answer overnight would red an untouched commit. So the judgement is a PURE function over recorded API responses and the fixture spawns the SHIPPED SCRIPT twice with `--fixture` and `--now`: once on a response with PITR off and no completed backup, asserting exit 1 naming 'no recovery mechanism at all' AND that the hint states the lane cannot test a restore; once on a PITR response, asserting exit 0 — so the red is the recorded posture and not a broken script. Two further spawns cover the credential path: an unconfigured tree exits 0 with a SKIP that must SAY 'NO backup evidence is being produced' (a silent skip would read as evidence), and the same tree with HARNESS_REQUIRE_BACKUP_EVIDENCE=1 exits 1. THE ASSERTIONS THAT MATTER MOST ARE THE ONES DEMANDING GREEN, and each encodes a documented vendor behaviour a naive control would red a CORRECT project over: PITR with zero daily backups (the vendor stops taking them when PITR is on, so the predicate is an OR and never an AND); an IDLE PITR project whose latest recovery point is three weeks stale (no activity means no WAL backups, and that recovery point still reflects current state); a project reporting RESTORING, PAUSING, RESIZING, COMING_UP or INACTIVE (asserting there would fire at the exact moment the operator is using what the lane protects); and a project younger than the operator's own tolerance, a guard that reuses THEIR number and invents none. The shape half is anti-vacuity: a response missing any of the five required fields, a status outside the published enum, a non-array `backups`, or a COMPLETED row whose `inserted_at` cannot be read as an unambiguous instant — that last one reported as a SHAPE problem specifically, because dropping the row would empty the newest-completed search and red the project for having no backups at all, the right verdict for entirely the wrong reason.

sbom-inventory.note: The asset-inventory lane (0.10.0), and the ONE lane in this workflow whose red-proof is not a vendor-shaped disclaimer — because unlike osv-scanner and gitleaks, the judgement here is code this repository owns. `pnpm sbom` is one line and cannot go red, so a lane that only EMITS an inventory is a green tick over an artefact that may have silently lost half the tree; check-sbom.mjs closes the emission against pnpm-lock.yaml in BOTH directions and the fixtures prove each. Under-reporting reds naming the absent packages (the inventory a scan is aimed at has a hole in it); OVER-reporting reds naming the foreign components (the artefact describes a different tree — a stale commit, a stray --filter, a generator pointed at another workspace — and a too-large inventory reads as thorough, which is why that arm exists at all). ANTI-VACUITY on both inputs, because each of them makes an empty set match an empty set and report clean: a zero-component SBOM is a hard red rather than a dependency-free repository, and a lockfile the parser found no `packages:` entries in is a hard red rather than a clean tree — and when both are gone the closure STOPS instead of adding noise about the comparison it could not make. A non-CycloneDX document reds and stops for the same reason. The spawned script proves the exit codes in both directions on one fixture set (a truncated inventory exits 1 with the FIX line, the complete one exits 0), so the red is not consistent with a script that always fails, and it proves the absent-lockfile asymmetry — loud local SKIP, hard CI failure. One test deliberately runs the REAL `pnpm sbom` over this repository and asserts the real closure is clean over it: the fixtures prove the judgement, and that test is the only thing that would notice a CycloneDX field rename or a pnpm change that stopped emitting components, both of which would leave every fixture green.

This is the one gate family whose subject is a CLAIM rather than a control — 149 rows stating how a generated application stands against ASD Maturity Level Three — so the injections are the REGRADE attempts, because the cheapest way to fake conformance is not to weaken a control but to relabel a row. Covered: a deleted row reds naming its strategy and both counts (the census, per Appendix C); the three superseded ML1/ML2 requirements must stay RECORDED and must not also be counted (the 152-vs-149 trap); an `effective` row naming a control nothing runs reds, and a CONDITIONAL control must disclose (path-filtered) or (schedule-gated) because existing and having-run are different claims; `alternate-control` without assessorMayRefuse reds (never pre-earned by a generator), `not-implemented` without an obligation reds (the register cannot hide a gap), `not-applicable` without a negative proof reds (silence is not a proof), an organisation-boundary row may carry no outcome and must name an owner, and an unbuilt row cannot claim the top evidence tier; a second shared-clause instance claiming a control reds as double-counting, while DIVERGENT outcomes across one clause must stay green (identical text, different subject stream — forcing equality would inflate three rows or deflate one); enabling [storage] or discovering an upload route reds because eleven macro grades rest on there being no document-parsing surface; and a simulated-activity claim with a missing or unregistered canary reds, which is this check's own subject. The shipped register is the clean case, so the proofs run against a real tree rather than a fixture. 0.10.0 WIDENS THE SUBJECT from the five simulated-activity rows to all ELEVEN positive claims (effective union alternate-control), because the old scope left an escape that cost nothing to take: grade yourself `effective`, claim a LOWER evidence tier, name no proof, stay green — the tier records how GOOD the evidence is and the closure was asking whether there is any, so scoping one to the other let a positive claim opt out of being falsifiable by admitting weaker evidence. Injections: an `effective` row at system-generated-artefact with its canary deleted reds (the escape itself), an `alternate-control` row is held to the same bar, and — the arm that keeps the widening from being cosmetic — a row citing ANOTHER gate’s real proof reds, because otherwise any row could name `tenancy`, resolve cleanly, and report a proven claim about a gate it never ran. The inverse holds too: a row grading nothing may not cite a red-proof, since evidence for a claim nobody made reads as a claim. The registry union is steps ∪ lanes, and one test pins WHY by running the closure against steps{} alone and asserting the four lane-backed rows red — under the 0.9.9 scope they could not have named a proof at all, which is the shape in which a widened closure gets weakened to fit rather than met. release.yml#release.note: 0.7.0 (W8): the publish-blocking wait is scripts/ci/wait-for-workflows.mjs — release blocks on green selftest.yml AND lint.yml runs at the tag SHA (tag-time parity) — and these are its death-tests: all-green → 0, any all-failed → hard fail naming it, still-running → keep polling, ZERO runs for a required workflow → hard fail after the timeout (absence-as-pending-forever is the silent-skip shape). The job's remaining inline steps — check-syntax, hygiene, check-release-lockstep, the full node --test suite — are proven in #factoryGates; hygiene.yml stays deliberately unawaited, with the reason written at the invocation.

scorecard.yml#analysis.note: OSSF Scorecard, a vendor posture-measurement lane publishing to the security tab; the verdict is the vendor action's, and the reason-to-exist is supply-chain posture measurement, not a blocking gate

selftest.yml#installer-unit.note: runs five factory gates (syntax, hygiene, release-lockstep, plugin-manifest — proven in #factoryGates), THIS CHECKER in full spawn mode, and the whole suite under coverage floors on ubuntu AND windows — the job is the execution vehicle for every fixture proof in this registry

selftest.yml#render-smoke.note: init on real scratch dirs (core + metal) then check-residue and check-syntax on each; the lifecycle suite is where the render/residue logic is proven red-able, and the lane proves it on a REAL rendered scaffold

selftest.yml#canary.note: 0.7.0: the job's baseline is DERIVED by scripts/ci/run-stop-chain.mjs, and these are its death-tests — a provenBy string absent from selftest.yml reds, exclusions are reviewed data with reasons. The job then executes the 'Canary <n>:' injections that #steps selftest-kind proofs grep-match into this workflow.

selftest.yml#canary-mutation.note: the job IS an executed red-proof: one untested branch must red the mutation lane while every other gate stays green — registered as the #lanes mutation selftest proof ('an untested branch must red the mutation lane')

selftest.yml#bootstrap-linux.note: a real scaffold plus the live Supabase stack: the full chain, the Stop chain as a chain via the real hook, and the live canaries (17, 18, 22, 23, 24) that #steps/#lanes selftest-kind proofs grep-match into this workflow — deleting any of those steps reds the grep, which is this job's staleness guard

selftest.yml#metal-bootstrap.note: the metal design-token variant of the bootstrap job: proves the second token set renders and validates through the same proven chain on its own scaffold

selftest.yml#upgrade-linux.note: the five-leg upgrade matrix via scripts/ci/upgrade-lane.sh; its expiry judgement (fired vs expected, the 'expected-but-silent' defect class) lives in scripts/lib/ramp-verdict.mjs precisely so these death-tests can falsify it

0.7.0: leg E's multi-version sweep set is computed by scripts/ci/upgrade-sweep.mjs over a reviewed SWEEPS table — a crossed version withholding files with no entry throws, and the (0.3.0, 0.6.0) set is pinned byte-identical to the single-version behavior it replaced

selftest.yml#consumer-ci-static.note: 0.9.0: the job IS an executed red/green pair — scripts/ci/consumer-ci-static.sh must see the exact frozen-lockfile refusal on the commit-before-install order AND complete the shipped static job (install + validate --min-floor) on a tree that followed init's next-steps note literally; registered as the #lanes static selftest proof. Schedule/dispatch only until its first runner green (the per-PR promotion is a recorded 0.10.0 obligation); the per-commit static closure over the same claims is check-ci-preconditions.mjs, proven in #factoryGates.

selftest.yml#integration.note: runs the scaffold's LIVE_PROOF suite against a real server and Postgres; its red-proof is Canary C01 (strip the Authorization header), registered as the #lanes integration-lane selftest proof

selftest.yml#maestro-smoke.note: the emulator canaries (19, 20) on a real Android emulator, schedule/dispatch-only for cost — registered as the #lanes mobile-e2e and perf-lane selftest proofs, which grep-match their leg titles into this workflow
